lesson.title: Gain of One, Value of Everything: The Voltage Follower
lesson.summary: The voltage follower is the non-inverting amplifier's limiting case, with the feedback resistor shorted to zero, giving a closed-loop gain of exactly 1 so the output simply tracks the input voltage.
lesson.body:
Take the non-inverting amplifier's gain formula from the previous chapter, Vout = Vin times (1 + R2 / R1), and consider the limiting case where R2 is replaced by a plain wire (R2 = 0 ohms) connecting the output directly back to the inverting input, with R1 removed entirely, so there is no path to ground pulling current out of that node. The gain becomes Av = 1 + 0 / (no resistor needed) = 1. It is easier to see directly: with the output wired straight to V-, the virtual short forces V- = V+ = Vin, and since V- is literally the same node as Vout, it follows immediately that Vout = Vin.

This gives a closed-loop gain of exactly 1, recalling the closed-loop gain chapter's result that the closed-loop gain approaches 1 / beta as open-loop gain grows large. Here the entire output is fed back (beta = 1), so 1 / beta = 1, consistent with the direct derivation.

As a numeric check, if Vin = 3.3 V, then Vout = 3.3 V, exactly, under the ideal assumptions. There is no interesting arithmetic here, and that is precisely the point worth dwelling on: a circuit that does not change the voltage at all can still be extremely useful, because voltage is not the only thing this circuit changes.

What the voltage follower does change is current and impedance. The source connected to V+ supplies almost no current, since the op-amp's input impedance is enormous (ideally infinite). Meanwhile, the op-amp's output, with its ideally zero output impedance, can supply whatever current a load demands while holding its voltage steady at Vin. In effect, a fragile, high-impedance signal is copied onto a robust, low-impedance output that can drive real loads without the source itself ever having to supply meaningful current. This impedance-transforming role, rather than any change in voltage, is exactly what earns this circuit its more descriptive name and its own dedicated chapter next: the buffer amplifier.
